reference.source: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
clinicalPearls: An umbrella term for a group of congenital, non-progressive disorders caused by abnormal development or connectivity (dysinnervation) of one or more cranial nerve nuclei and their nerves, rather than by primary muscle disease

The group includes Duane retraction syndrome, congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, Mobius syndrome, horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, congenital ptosis, hereditary congenital facial paresis and Marcus Gunn jaw-winking synkinesis
Hallmarks are aberrant innervation and synkinesis, for example globe retraction with palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction in Duane, or lid elevation with jaw movement in Marcus Gunn

Many have identified genetic causes affecting axon guidance and neuronal development, including KIF21A and TUBB3 (CFEOM), CHN1 (Duane), ROBO3 (horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis), and SALL4 and HOXA1
Secondary muscle fibrosis and restriction, with positive forced ductions, are common because the muscles develop abnormally following the primary dysinnervation

Diagnosis rests on recognising the characteristic pattern of restricted or aberrant motility, associated synkinesis and any systemic or skeletal features, with high-resolution MRI sometimes showing hypoplastic or absent cranial nerves
Some forms are isolated and purely ocular, whereas others are syndromic with skeletal (scoliosis, limb), auditory or neurodevelopmental features
Management is largely supportive and surgical (alignment, ptosis and head-posture correction) with genetic counselling, as the underlying dysinnervation cannot be reversed
reference.pathophysiology: The congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders arise from maldevelopment of cranial motor neurons and/or their axonal pathways during embryogenesis, producing absent, deficient or misdirected (aberrant) innervation of the ocular, facial and other cranial-nerve-supplied muscles. Causative genes encode proteins for axon guidance, motor-neuron specification and cytoskeletal function, for example ROBO3 (midline axon crossing) in horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, CHN1 (alpha-2-chimaerin, axon guidance) in Duane, PHOX2A and MAFB (motor-neuron and nucleus development), and KIF21A and TUBB3 (axonal transport and microtubule structure) in CFEOM. Aberrant reinnervation produces the characteristic synkinetic movements, while abnormal muscle development leads to secondary fibrosis and restriction. The disorders are congenital and non-progressive, with rare exceptions such as the progressive scoliosis component of HGPPS.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired cranial nerve palsies (traumatic, ischaemic, compressive or inflammatory)
Myasthenia gravis and congenital myasthenic syndromes
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia and mitochondrial myopathies
Congenital myopathies with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis
Thyroid eye disease and other orbital restrictive disease
Isolated comitant strabismus and refractive or accommodative squint
Brainstem malformations and posterior fossa lesions
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution thin-section MRI of the brainstem, orbits and cranial nerves
Orthoptic assessment of ductions, alignment, synkinesis and head posture
Forced duction and force generation testing to identify restriction
Targeted genetic testing, gene panels or exome (for example KIF21A, TUBB3, CHN1, ROBO3, HOXA1, SALL4)
Spinal imaging for scoliosis (for example in suspected HGPPS) and a skeletal survey if syndromic
Audiological and neurodevelopmental assessment where relevant
Cardiac, renal and limb evaluation in syndromic forms such as SALL4-related disease
redFlags: A progressive course or new neurological deficit, suggesting an acquired or alternative diagnosis
Progressive scoliosis with a horizontal gaze palsy (HGPPS), requiring spinal monitoring
Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk, as in the Mobius spectrum
Corneal exposure from lagophthalmos or a poor Bell's phenomenon
Systemic features indicating a syndromic genetic cause that requires multisystem work-up
reference.prognosis: These disorders are congenital and non-progressive, so vision and function are generally stable, and multidisciplinary and surgical management improves alignment, head posture, lid position and cosmesis. The aberrant innervation and associated motility limitation usually persist, and prognosis in syndromic forms depends on the associated systemic features.
pitfalls: Treating a dysinnervation disorder as a primary muscle problem and missing the neurogenic basis
Overlooking synkinesis, for example not testing adduction for globe retraction in Duane or jaw movement in Marcus Gunn
Failing to screen for syndromic or systemic features such as scoliosis, hearing loss, limb and cardiac anomalies
Not counselling families about the genetic basis and recurrence risk
Expecting surgery to restore normal motility rather than to improve head posture and alignment
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Correct significant ocular misalignment, abnormal head posture and globe retraction with strabismus surgery, addressing coexisting muscle restriction
Perform ptosis surgery such as a frontalis sling for vision-threatening ptosis and manage Marcus Gunn jaw-winking synkinesis surgically where troublesome
Optimise vision during development with refractive correction and amblyopia therapy
Use prisms and orthoptic measures for residual gaze and alignment abnormalities and to relieve abnormal head posture
Manage associated features including scoliosis in horizontal gaze palsy, corneal protection and lubrication for facial paresis in Mobius syndrome, and feeding or airway support where needed
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across paediatric ophthalmology, neurology, orthopaedics and clinical genetics
Offer genetic counselling given identified heritable causes such as KIF21A, TUBB3, CHN1 and ROBO3
